chunks.text: 3 Methodology 3.1 Model Architecture Overview Fig. 2 shows the architecture of the proposed ReSEViT, which is a three-stage model. Each stage is composed of a residual token embedding and a convolution transformer block [ cvt ] . In this section, we describe our multi-stage ViT design for small-data image classification tasks. 3.1.1 Residual Token Embedding We replace the convolution token of CvT [ cvt ] with the residual token, which is a ResNet block [ resnet ] for effective local structures where the stronger local representations constitute the locality inductive bias provided to the Transformer. Convolution is an important factor in extracting local structures related to small-scale design in ViT. Generally, convolution layers transform the features by using a deep structure. Given the input image, the first convolutional layer extracts low-level features of the object. When the second or subsequent convolution layer is piled, the features transformed into higher-level features. Based on the convolution output characteristics, the skip connection ensures the network does not forget the lower-level feature. Otherwise, the feature representation becomes too abstract due to deep convolutions. In Fig. 3 , the residual token captures clearer edges, contours, and texture patterns highlighted in stage 1. Moreover, compared with the convolution token, the residual token increasingly focuses on the object and highlights distinct parts, such as the head and body, rather than the background in stage 2. In stage 3, activations in residual token form more coherent patterns corresponding to regions of the object, not only scattered pixels. First, the CLS token is added to each transformer block as a feature representation. The CLS token is then fed to the stage classifier. For general purposes, we also design early-stage classifier architectures for other deep learning models, whose architectures are similar to their deepest-stage classifiers. For example, the ResNet18 stage classifier consists of global max pooling followed by a fully connected (FC) layer. In general, the entire structure of the stage classifiers remains identical. As such, the additional parameters are from the FC layer of each stage classifier when the self-ensemble method is applied.

For efficiency, no convolution layer is involved in all stage classifier designs, including our model and other general models, to explore its effects on the base classifiers. 3.2 Self-Ensemble Learning Similar to the motivation of skip connections, the self-ensemble method ensures that the model prediction result keeps the essential part of the early-stage classifier prediction results if the early-stage classifiers are also supervised during training. The earlier stage classifier prediction results are influenced by the lower-level feature, while the subsequent stage classifier prediction results are influenced by the higher-level feature. Implicitly, the self-ensemble is responsible for global information flow ( all stages ), while the residual token embedding is responsible for local information flow ( each individual stage ). In this sense, when the local information flow is stronger, it will be beneficial for the global information flow. We further propose the self-ensemble method, as shown in the red dashed line of Fig. 2 . Specifically, we ensemble the results from different stages as follows: k ⋆ = arg ​ max k = 1 K ⁡ 1 N ​ ∑ n = 1 N Z n , k , k^{\star}=\argmax^{K}_{k=1}\frac{1}{N}\sum^{N}_{n=1}Z_{n,k}, (5) where Z n Z_{n} is the n n -th classifier probability distribution output, n = 1 , … , N n=1,...,N , k = 1 , … , K k=1,...,K , k ⋆ k^{\star} is the optimal class, N N is the number of stage classifiers, and K K is the number of classes. In Eq. ( 5 ), the multiple predictions are averaged, and then arg ​ max \argmax is used to return the maximum value among the class indices for a class decision. Theoretically, ViT requires large datasets due to its weak inductive biases, making it prone to overfitting on small datasets. Self-ensemble learning can alleviate this problem by aggregating multiple predictions. Consequently, the prediction variance is reduced, leading to better generalization.

Assuming the variance of the self-ensemble can be simplified as: V ​ a ​ r ​ ( Z ^ ) = σ 2 ​ ( ρ + 1 − ρ N ) , Var(\hat{Z})=\sigma^{2}\bigg(\rho+\frac{1-\rho}{N}\bigg), (6) where Z ^ \hat{Z} is the final ensemble prediction; σ 2 \sigma^{2} is the variance of an individual prediction; ρ \rho is the average pairwise correlation between ensemble predictions. Eq. 6 indicates that as N N increases and ρ < 1 \rho<1 , the prediction variance can be reduced, leading to improved generalization, particularly on small datasets, where high variance contributes to overfitting. 3.2.1 Multistage Ensemble Loss A naïve ensemble might degrade the model performance due to the absence of supervision on early-stage classifiers. In other words, the importance of early-stage classifiers is adaptive since they may offer important information in some cases while acting as noise in other cases. To update the model weights for each stage classifier directly from the true label, we propose the multistage ensemble loss. Given training samples X = { x , y } X=\{x,y\} , where x x is the input image, and y y is the true label, the probability distribution output of each stage classifier is supervised by the true label y y , i.e. , ℒ S ​ E = 1 N ​ ∑ n = 1 N ℒ C ​ E ​ ( Z n , y ) , \mathcal{L}_{SE}=\frac{1}{N}\sum^{N}_{n=1}\mathcal{L}_{CE}(Z_{n},y), (7) where ℒ S ​ E \mathcal{L}_{SE} represents self-ensemble loss and ℒ C ​ E \mathcal{L}_{CE} is the label smoothing cross-entropy loss. 3.2.2 Dynamic Learner Selection (DLS) With the multistage ensemble loss, the early-stage classifiers perform better than a setting that uses a single loss. However, we argue that the outputs of different stages should not have the same importance. Therefore, we further propose Dynamic Learner Selection (DLS) to adaptively adjust the stage-classifier weights.

The goal of the DLS is to maximize the use of best stage classifiers while minimizing the stage classifiers with an inferior performance by adding priority scores β \beta , which is based on the training accuracy over epochs of each stage classifier. It is simple and effective with no additional parameters. Concretely, let β n \beta_{n} and a ​ c ​ c n acc_{n} denote the weight of the n n -th stage classifier and the training accuracy of Z n Z_{n} , respectively. β n \beta_{n} can be calculated as follows: β n = a ​ c ​ c n ∑ n = 1 N a ​ c ​ c n + ϵ . \beta_{n}=\frac{acc_{n}}{\sum^{N}_{n=1}acc_{n}+\epsilon}. As shown in Table 4 , we conduct the following experiments on small-scale general datasets benchmark, i.e. , CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and Tiny-ImageNet. Tiny-ImageNet is a subset of the original ImageNet. As the small-scale datasets cover both small and large image resolution, we also conduct our experiments on ImageNet100, a subset of the ImageNet1K dataset [ imagenet ] . MedMNIST, a small-scale medical imaging dataset comprising 10 subsets with a 28 × \times 28 image resolution, is also used for evaluation. Moreover, ISIC 2018 is a skin lesion dataset containing 10,015 labeled images (450 × \times 600 resolution). The dataset is split into 80% training and 20% testing, and all images are resized to 224 × \times 224. Model Variants. We develop three variants of ReSEViT on small-scale datasets with different sizes, such as ReSEViT-T (tiny), ReSEViT-S (small), and ReSEViT-L (large), as shown in Table 3 . Both ReSEViT-T and ReSEViT-S are evaluated on small-resolution image datasets. On the other hand, ReSEViT-L is designed for a large-resolution image dataset. Three stages are employed. h n h_{n} denotes the head number of each stage, s s is the stride of convolution, s k , v s_{k,v} denotes the stride of key and value, and T n T_{n} is the token sequence length. Implementation Details. During training, AdamW [ adamW ] is used as the optimizer with a weight decay of 3e-2.

We train our models for 200 epochs with a batch size of 64, an initial learning rate of 5e-4, a cosine learning rate scheduler [ cosinelr ] , and label smoothing with a probability of 0.1. While training, our methods are warmed up for 10 epochs. For data augmentation, we use horizontal flipping, random cropping, and AutoAugment [ autoaugment ] . For Tiny-ImageNet, the stride of the convolutional stem in all models is doubly increased (from 1 to 2) to accommodate the 32 × \times 32 receptive field, hence, the computational complexity remains equivalent. For ImageNet100 and ISIC 2018, we train from scratch for 100 epochs with a batch size of 64. All experimental results are averaged over three runs. For comparison, prior method results are reported or trained with our training setting when the official implementation is publicly available. Table 5 compares our approach with CNN-based and ViT models in various aspects, i.e. , accuracy and efficiency. ViT: Based on the result, we can see that ViT-B underperforms with its pure transformer architecture.

Since the input size is 32 × \times 32, we report another different patch size from 16 × \times 16 to 4 × \times 4, resulting in a quadratic increase in the FLOPs (12.8 × \times ) and low inference throughput (3.7 × \times ). This is because the number of tokens directly affects the input sequence length from 4 to 64 to the transformer layers. The ViT result shows that smaller patch sizes for the transformer still cannot really compete with the hybrid ViT in a light computational budget with a limited amount of data, indicating a data-hunger. Hybrid ViT: Compared with CvT-13 † as the hybrid ViT base form, our ReSEViT-T achieves 4.61% better performance while improving its efficiency because the residual token and self-ensemble method suggest local and global information flows. NesT-T performs better than the CvT-13 † , CCT-7/3 × \times 1, and TransXNet-T † in accuracy performance with the nested architecture and local translations, but the throughput speed is much slower. Our ReSEViT-T achieves better performance than NesT-T by 1.42%, while the model size is more compact and the throughput is faster. Area Under the Curve (AUC) and Top-1 accuracy are chosen as metrics due to the common class imbalance issue present in the MedMNIST sub-datasets [ smalldatasetaugmentation ] . In this experiment, the model with the highest AUC on the validation set is selected for the test. Based on the results, we observe that ReSEViT-T outperforms the other ViT variants in the small-scale medical domain.

Besides the MedMNIST benchmark, we also conducted a comparative evaluation of ViT variants on the ISIC 2018 image dataset in Table 8 , where the proposed approach attained the highest AUC and accuracy among the evaluated ViT models. The experimental results also confirm that the self-ensemble components, particularly DLS, effectively enhance the overall performance. 4.5 Gradient Norm Analysis for Model Interpretation By comparing gradient norms across token variants and learning methods in the ReSEViT model throughout training, we examine whether certain methods yield more stable gradient magnitudes, potentially facilitating more effective gradient propagation and optimization. In Fig. 5 , we observe that across most methods, gradient norms peak in Stage 1 and then decrease progressively in subsequent stages as the earlier stages are more sensitive to the input and receive stronger gradient signals. This indicates a problem when the gradients are excessively large and unstable. The ML method can further increase the gradient magnitude by accumulating gradients from multiple exit losses. To address this issue, the imbalance in gradients can be substantially reduced by the residual token and the DLS module indicating that the gradients are effectively stabilized and regulated without making them vanished. This effect is crucial particularly for small datasets, where ViT models receive less diverse supervision and are more sensitive to optimization instability. By maintaining a balanced gradient propagation across stages, residual token and DLS can improve the reliability of feature learning under limited data. It arises when ViT performs poorly on limited image data. Our self-ensemble learning alleviates the issue by leveraging information from the intermediate classifiers for global information flow. Self-ensemble learning reduces prediction variance, which can improve model generalization, especially in small-data settings. As the importance of multi-stages is not the same, we introduced DLS to optimize our ensemble performance by decision fusion weights. The DLS is proven to reduce calibration error and stabilize the gradient. To improve global information flows, we incorporate residual tokens that model stronger local structures in each model exit. The residual token can capture clearer object features that can benefit the Transformer.

Unifying residual tokens and self-ensemble learning into a multi-stage ViT facilitates a more efficient computational framework reducing redundancy, prediction error, and variance. Experimental results have demonstrated that the proposed method outperforms previous methods efficiently through the multi-stage ViT design and self-ensemble learning on small image datasets. A.3.1 Performance Results on Class Imbalance We observe that ReSEViT-T outperforms the other model architectures in Top-1 accuracy across different r r . Additionally, the proposed self-ensemble and DLS modules work well even under different r r . As the dataset becomes highly imbalanced, the performance degradation of our modules remains relatively stable. A.4 Roadmap Design for Small Dataset In this section, we present a detailed projection for multi-stage ViT design from CvT-13 to ReSEViT-T that is used for small-data image classification in Table 18 . As shown, the design retains its final shape from ResNet18 to ReSEViT-T, bridging the gap between the ResNet and the Transformer. Moreover, it has been acknowledged that when the deep learning model’s performance improves, the model size will also be larger. In this work, we optimize our multi-stage ViT design to achieve the ideal equilibrium between accuracy and efficiency. A.4.1 Patchify Originally, the CvT-13 [ cvt ] was designed for large resolution images and had an original convolutional stem of 7 × \times 7 kernel size with 4 strides to reduce the input from 224 × \times 224 to 56 × \times 56. For the small-resolution input design (32 × \times 32), we replace it with a 3 × \times 3 kernel size with 1 stride to increase the effective receptive fields. As a result, the accuracy is drastically improved by 15.08% showing that stem design is important for a small-resolution input size.

A.4.2 Stage Ratio Afterward, the stage ratio between convolution channel size and transformer depth into the base form is shrunk as the parameter size and the FLOPs are excessive for small-scale datasets compared with CCT-7/3 × \times 1 and Nest-T (around 3-6M parameter size). Specifically, the convolution channel size is reduced from [64,192,384] to [64,128,256], and the transformer depth is reduced from [1,2,10] to [1,1,1]. The base network becomes super fast and light, but the performance reduces by 5.87%. A.4.3 Local Information Flow To compensate for the ideal computational budget, we substitute the convolution token with the residual token. As the 4 th stage of ResNet18 with 512 channel size is redundant for small-scale design (significantly increases the parameters to 11.22M), we reconstruct it with the same design principle of CvT-13 to the three-stage model. Notably, the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency is decent. Specifically, the parameter size and FLOPs are comparable with other ViTs [ cct , nest ] , and the accuracy increases by 9.96%. Afterward, residual tokens and convolution tokens with wider channel sizes from [64, 128, 256] to [128, 256, 512] are also compared. We observe that the residual token outperforms wider convolution token as the Transformer is able to process stronger local structures more effectively.
